headline: Strike on Saudi wealth fund tower and Iranian raids on Bahrain jolt Gulf's postwar mood
bottomLine: A suspected Houthi missile strike that damaged the Riyadh tower housing the Public Investment Fund, Iran's third round of strikes on Bahrain and a tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz reverse last week's 'effectively over' narrative and bring the war to the doorstep of a sovereign wealth fund. Markets have so far looked through it, with Brent roughly flat at $92.94 and the riyal pinned near 3.75, but a 1.5% slide in the Egyptian pound to 54.19 per dollar shows where risk premia are starting to surface. Buffers are uneven: Qatar's current-account surplus of 14.8% of GDP and Saudi growth of 4.5% contrast with inflation of 14.1% in Egypt and 34.9% in Turkey, and a 5.3% of GDP deficit in Jordan (2024), leaving importers most exposed if Hormuz or Red Sea disruption persists.
notableFlows: The Abu Dhabi Investment Council, a Mubadala unit, reportedly exited 19 stocks in its latest filing while keeping every share of BlackRock's IBIT bitcoin ETF, which now makes up about 54% of its reported book. The concentration marks a striking shift in Gulf sovereign portfolio strategy, though the figures come from a filing-based secondary report and have not been confirmed by the fund.

An Abu Dhabi wealth fund is among the anchor investors, alongside India's LIC, in the Mahanadi Coalfields IPO. The participation shows Gulf sovereign capital still seeking South Asian energy-linked assets even as regional security deteriorates, although the size of its allocation was not disclosed.

Shipping risk is rising on both of the Gulf's maritime arteries: a tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, according to UKMTO, and Yemeni forces' retreat has left the Houthis in control of a key Red Sea waterway. With Brent flat at $92.94, the market is not yet pricing a supply disruption, but freight and insurance costs are the first channel through which Egypt and Jordan would feel it.

The missile strike that damaged the PIF's Riyadh tower raises operational and insurance questions for the kingdom's main investment vehicle, and BBC reports that AI-generated fakes about the attack have spread widely. There is no evidence so far that the strike has affected PIF's deal-making, but it makes the fund's headquarters a symbol of Gulf financial exposure to the war.

risks.title: Gulf war re-escalates against financial and military targets
risks.description: Since last week: Washington's 'effectively over' assessment has been undercut by Iran's third round of strikes on Bahrain, home of the US Navy's 5th Fleet, reported Iranian attacks on US bases in Gulf countries, a tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz and a suspected Houthi missile strike that damaged the PIF tower in Riyadh. The war is now nine months old and has reached the Saudi capital's financial district. Brent at $92.94 is flat, so the market is pricing contained disruption and remains exposed if Hormuz traffic is hit.

risks.title: Red Sea control and external pressure on Egypt and Jordan
risks.description: Since last week: Yemeni forces' retreat has left the Houthis in control of a key Red Sea waterway, and the Egyptian pound has weakened 1.5% to 54.19 per dollar. Egypt combines 14.1% inflation with a 3.8% of GDP current-account deficit, while Jordan's deficit was 5.3% of GDP in 2024. Both would feel any rise in freight, insurance or energy costs quickly.

risks.title: COP31 deadlock over fossil fuels
risks.description: COP31 is reported to be on the brink of collapse after the EU rejected a UN climate deal amid a row with Saudi Arabia over fossil fuels. A failed outcome would prolong uncertainty over long-run demand and carbon-policy assumptions in Gulf hydrocarbon planning, though it has no immediate effect on output or prices.
